turns.en: I asked you, what are some counterintuitive lessons that you've learned that go against common startup wisdom?
turns.zh: 我问过你，有哪些反直觉的经验教训，是违背常见创业智慧的？

turns.en: I'm no longer beholden to any corporate comms team right now, so I can let it rip a little bit.
turns.zh: 我现在不再受任何企业公关团队的约束，所以我可以稍微放开一点。

turns.en: You like to design teams like a terrorist organization. A good terrorist organization essentially has two things. One is it has this ideological culture that everyone understands why they are doing what they're doing. And then it has a very very clear organizational structure of who can be trusted with which decision.
turns.zh: 你喜欢像设计恐怖组织一样设计团队。一个好的恐怖组织本质上具备两点。一是它有一种意识形态文化，每个人都明白自己为什么做正在做的事。然后它有一个非常非常清晰的组织结构，明确谁可以被信任做出哪个决定。

turns.en: You like to spend time writing your best people into the ground versus improving the average people.
turns.zh: 你喜欢花时间把你最优秀的人用到极致，而不是去提升普通的人。

turns.en: If you see somebody drowning, you want to save them. I did the absolute opposite. If somebody is strong and crushing it, I'm just handing them more and more rope to hang themselves with.
turns.zh: 如果你看到有人溺水，你会想救他们。我做的恰恰相反。如果某人很强并且表现出色，我只会给他们越来越多的绳子让他们自己上吊。

turns.en: Something that I know you believe. Most product managers are bad and are often net negative to the company.
turns.zh: 我知道你相信的一点。大多数产品经理都很糟糕，并且常常对公司净负面。

turns.en: The great product managers are exiting the system. They're becoming founders. They're becoming executives. It's kind of set up to be this profession where the median product manager is actually probably pretty bad.
turns.zh: 伟大的产品经理正在离开这个体系。他们成为创始人。他们成为高管。这个职业的设置方式使得中位数产品经理实际上可能相当糟糕。

turns.en: Snap is quite famous for not hiring PMs for a long time.
turns.zh: Snap 因为长时间不招聘产品经理而相当出名。

turns.en: The baseline is we should just be able to operate this product without any product manager. So, this person has to provide value over nobody.
turns.zh: 基线是我们应该能够在没有任何产品经理的情况下运营这个产品。所以，这个人必须提供比没有人更多的价值。

turns.en: Feels like an interesting new skill for PMs is pushing back on things AI adding to your products.
turns.zh: 感觉产品经理的一个有趣新技能是抵制 AI 添加到你的产品中的东西。

turns.en: I think I saw Evan personally say no to better ideas than I've seen almost any other consumer startup launch. Exercising that kind of muscle of saying no of restraint is probably one of the few muscles of taste you can exercise. If a museum has all of their collection on the walls then the curator hasn't done anything.
turns.zh: 我认为我亲眼看到 Evan 个人拒绝的好主意，比我在几乎所有其他消费创业公司发布中看到的都要多。锻炼那种说不、克制的肌肉，可能是你能锻炼的少数品味肌肉之一。如果博物馆把所有藏品都挂在墙上，那么策展人什么也没做。

turns.en: The first thing I want to talk about, something that stood out in our jamming on what to talk about is uh the way you think about designing teams. The way you described it to me is you like to design teams like a terrorist organization.
turns.zh: 我想谈的第一件事，在我们讨论要谈什么时突出的，是呃你思考设计团队的方式。你向我描述的方式是你喜欢像设计恐怖组织一样设计团队。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I should probably workshop this one a little bit.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。我可能应该稍微修改一下这个说法。

turns.en: This is probably an example of the one that's better for behind closed doors. But yeah, when I actually talked to the chief people officer at Discord about this, I think she was simultaneously horrified and intrigued, in a way — credit to her for not judging me right off the bat. I think it comes from essentially two primary beliefs from me. One is that there's actually a hidden cost to collaborating that no one really internalizes extremely well. Meaning, you'll never hear any executive at any company be like, "Stop collaborating." And to me, that's kind of a warning sign. Collaboration comes with incredible coordination costs. And coordination costs essentially assure that you're moving as slow as the slowest node in the system. So I try and aggressively internalize the cost of collaboration sometimes.
turns.zh: 这大概就是那种更适合关起门来说的例子。不过，当我和 Discord 的首席人力官聊到这件事时，我觉得她既惊恐又好奇——某种程度上，得感谢她没有一上来就评判我。我认为这本质上来自我的两个核心信念。第一，协作其实有一种隐藏成本，没有人真正把它内化得很好。意思是，你永远不会听到任何公司的高管说“别协作了”。对我来说，这本身就是个警示信号。协作伴随着惊人的协调成本。而协调成本基本上保证了你的速度会和系统里最慢的那个节点一样慢。所以我有时会试着激进地把协作的成本内化掉。

turns.en: And then the second thing, separately from this, is that at high-growth companies especially — and so many of the people who listen to your podcast aspire to be at these types of companies — product managers should be in a position where they're making decisions that the founders would have made, like, six months ago, definitely a year or two ago. These are decisions that the founders themselves would have made. So, set aside violence for a moment — I'm not saying that I designed my teams for violence. But a good terrorist organization essentially has two things. One, it has this ideological culture where everyone understands why they are doing what they're doing. And then it has a very, very clear organizational structure of who can be trusted with which decision. I think creating a culture where there's a very clear, almost religious-level ideological goal — the strategy is almost like a religion to the entire team — and an organizational structure where people understand who the directly responsible individuals are, who's single-threaded on something, who's the throat to choke, use whatever MBA-ism you want — I think the combination of those two things can be leveraged in a way such that you don't need to over-collaborate and you can be assured of achieving the results that you wanted as if you had collaborated.
turns.zh: 然后第二点，和这个分开来看，尤其是在高增长公司——你的播客的很多听众都渴望进入这类公司——产品经理应该处于这样一个位置：他们做的决策，是创始人六个月前会做的决策，肯定也是一两年前会做的。这些是创始人自己会做的决策。所以，先把暴力放一边——我不是说我把团队设计成搞暴力的。但一个优秀的恐怖组织本质上具备两样东西。第一，它有一种意识形态文化，每个人都明白自己为什么在做正在做的事。第二，它有一个非常非常清晰的组织结构，规定谁可以被信任做哪个决策。我认为，创造这样一种文化——有一个非常清晰的、几乎宗教级别的意识形态目标，整个团队把战略几乎当成一种宗教——再加上一种组织结构，让人们明白谁是直接责任人，谁在某个事情上是单线程负责的，谁是那个可以问责的人，随便你用哪个 MBA 术语——我认为这两者的结合可以被利用起来，让你不需要过度协作，同时又能确保达到你想要的结果，就像你协作过一样。

turns.en: So I think the components of what is this great ideological setup — a lot of things I focus on, for example, because I think often the head of product at high-growth companies where the founders are still in charge — the head of product is really kind of a vessel for their vision. Both with Snap and at Discord, where I had the privilege of working with the founders in both cases, I tried to take and absorb and internalize their vision and then create small phrases and language that could be used and repeated, that were essentially shortcuts or almost like synecdoches of the whole strategy. So yeah, I could go more into that, but that's kind of how I think of it. And obviously giving it branding that, you know, I'm designing it like a terrorist organization at least gets people's attention. But maybe I need to workshop that a little bit.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，这个伟大的意识形态设定由哪些部分组成——比如我关注的很多方面，因为我认为在高增长公司里，当创始人仍然掌权时，产品负责人往往真的是他们愿景的一个载体。在 Snap 和 Discord，我都有幸与创始人共事，我试着去吸收、内化他们的愿景，然后创造一些可以被使用和重复的小短语和语言，它们本质上是整个战略的捷径，或者几乎像是提喻。所以，是的，我可以再深入讲，但这就是我大致思考的方式。显然，给它贴上品牌标签——你知道，我把它设计得像一个恐怖组织——至少能引起人们的注意。但也许我需要再打磨一下这个说法。

turns.en: No, you don't. This is perfect. This is exactly what I was hoping this conversation would be. So just to be very clear about the elements of the terrorist organization that we want to keep. One is this idea of autonomy, essentially kind of trusting people further down in case the leaders get caught or are incommunicative. So basically giving more autonomy to folks further down the chain. And then two is having a very clear mission ideology, you might say, so that everyone's very aligned and decisions are quick and that kind of thing.
turns.zh: 不，你不需要。这太完美了。这正是我希望这场对话会有的样子。所以，为了非常清楚地说明我们想保留的恐怖组织的要素。第一是自主性这个理念，本质上是信任更下层的人，以防领导者被抓或失联。所以基本上是给链条更下层的人更多自主权。第二是有一个非常清晰的使命意识形态，可以这么说，这样每个人都高度一致，决策也快，诸如此类。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And to be clear, I didn't start with "I'm going to build a terrorist organization." That I may—
turns.zh: 是的。是的。而且说清楚，我并不是一开始就说“我要建一个恐怖组织”。那我可能——

turns.en: I bet you built a great one, by the way.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我打赌你建了一个很棒的。

turns.en: That would be a great one. But when I thought about the elements of what I wanted from the organizations I was building, I couldn't help but notice that there were organizations out there operating like this, and they just so happen to be terrorist organizations. So yeah, that led to a lot of interesting reading lists. I think the Peter Sellis product reading list is almost like a banned book list at this point.
turns.zh: 那会是个很棒的。但当我思考我想从正在构建的组织中得到哪些要素时，我不禁注意到，外面有些组织就是这样运作的，而它们恰好是恐怖组织。所以，是的，这引出了很多有趣的阅读清单。我觉得 Peter Sellis 的产品阅读清单现在几乎像是一份禁书清单了。

turns.en: It's interesting because I've heard many people describe you want to build a cult, and this is not that different, because you know cults are very effective at getting stuff done.
turns.zh: 这很有意思，因为我听过很多人描述说你想建立一种邪教，而这和那个没什么不同，因为你知道邪教在把事情做成方面非常高效。

turns.en: It is not— Yeah, you can't spell culture without cult. And so I think yeah, it is not very different from that. I think there are elements of a cult that are more about the person leading the cult, whereas terrorist organizations are more about a higher power or like a religion or ideology. So that's why I tended more towards that. But yeah, I think you could read up on a couple of cults and then just take it all the way to the penultimate moment, like before they do the thing that makes them well known as a cult. And you probably could learn a lot. Honestly, there's a lot of alpha in that.
turns.zh: 并不是——是的，culture 这个词里没有 cult 就拼不出来。所以我认为，是的，它和那个没什么不同。我认为邪教有些要素更关乎领导邪教的那个人，而恐怖组织更关乎一种更高的力量，或者像宗教或意识形态。所以这就是为什么我更倾向于那个。但是的，我认为你可以读一些邪教的资料，然后一直推到倒数第二个时刻，就是他们做出那件让他们作为邪教闻名的事情之前。你大概能学到很多。老实说，那里面有很多 alpha。

turns.en: Speaking of a higher power, a fun fact about you is you managed Nikita Bier, who came on the podcast, one of the most popular episodes of the podcast, quite a character. Was head of product for X recently, for I think a year. Very few people have worked with Nikita. I'm curious what it was like to actually manage Nikita, work with Nikita.
turns.zh: 说到更高的力量，关于你的一个有趣事实是，你管理过 Nikita Bier，他上过这档播客，是最受欢迎的几期之一，相当有个性。他最近在 X 担任产品负责人，我想大概有一年。很少有人和 Nikita 共事过。我很好奇，真正管理 Nikita、和 Nikita 共事是什么感觉。

turns.en: Yeah, Nikita was on my team at Discord. We acquired his startup. And he was on the team at Discord for almost or over a year, with some phenomenal engineers that came along with him. I think managing Nikita — that's a very loose term, use of the word "manage." I think much like — yeah, you don't manage Nikita, you only seek to control him or direct him. I liken it a lot to — I mean, Nikita is an awesome personality and just actual operator in the product space, like pretty much one of one. And I have a ton of respect for a lot of the stuff that he does. I think of him a lot like Liam Neeson in the Taken movie series. Like, yeah, if your daughter gets kidnapped, he has a very special set of skills and he's going to employ those skills, and those skills are very hard to come by and very useful in certain situations. But then when you need him to raise the daughter or buy some groceries or stuff like that, all he knows how to do is just kill everybody in the grocery store or something like that.
turns.zh: 是的，Nikita 曾在 Discord 我的团队里。我们收购了他的创业公司。他在 Discord 团队待了将近一年多，还带来了一些非常出色的工程师。我觉得管理 Nikita——“管理”这个词用得非常宽松。我觉得很像——是的，你没法管理 Nikita，你只能试图控制他或引导他。我常把他比作——我是说，Nikita 是个很棒的个性，也是产品领域真正的操盘手，几乎独一无二。我对他做的很多事情都非常尊重。我常把他想成《飓风营救》系列电影里的 Liam Neeson。就像，是的，如果你女儿被绑架了，他有一套非常特殊的技能，他会动用那些技能，而那些技能非常难得，在某些情况下非常有用。但当你需要他抚养女儿，或者买点杂货之类的，他只会把杂货店里所有人都杀掉之类的。

turns.en: How do you feel about having folks like that in your team? A lot of people talk about having very distinct roles for different people, and sometimes you need someone like that.
turns.zh: 对于团队里有这样的人，你怎么看？很多人说要给不同的人非常明确的角色，有时候你就是需要这样的人。

turns.en: I think it's essential to be able to create an organization that can adopt that type of talent. I view it as a failure state if you have product orgs that can't handle really spiky talent. Nikita took it to extremes. You remember when he was on Intro doing that thing? At one point I was trying to get a one-on-one with him—who, by the way, reported up into me—and I couldn't get him. So I was like, dude, if you don't answer my DMs, I'm going to go on Intro and book you so I can just have a one-on-one with you right now.
turns.zh: 我认为，能够建立一个可以吸纳这类人才的组织，是至关重要的。如果你有产品组织无法驾驭那种非常“尖刺型”的人才，我会把它视为一种失败状态。Nikita 把这一点推到了极致。你记得他在 Intro 上做那件事的时候吗？有一次我想跟他约个一对一——顺便说一句，他是向我汇报的——但我约不到他。所以我就说，哥们，你要是再不回我私信，我就上 Intro 去预约你，这样我现在就能跟你一对一了。

turns.en: Luckily we didn't get to that. He answered. I think I hit him up on like four different messaging apps before I got a hold of him. But yeah, I think this ability to handle spikiness, to build teams that can adopt the type of talent that isn't necessarily the perfect nine-to-five employee from a product perspective—I look up a lot, from a management style perspective, to Phil Jackson, the coach of the Bulls and the Lakers. I think his ability to mesh talent of very different types that literally does not get along otherwise, to create these winning teams, to have done it both as a player and as a coach in two different places, to use philosophies from eastern philosophies, western philosophies, to combine all this stuff—I think he's one of the most meaningful leaders from a leadership styles perspective of the last half century.
turns.zh: 幸好我们没走到那一步。他回复了。我记得我在大概四个不同的通讯软件上找过他，才联系上他。但没错，我认为这种驾驭“尖刺型”人才的能力，这种打造能够吸纳那些从产品角度来说未必是完美朝九晚五员工的人才的团队的能力——从管理风格上来说，我非常仰慕菲尔·杰克逊，公牛队和湖人队的教练。我认为他能够把类型迥异、平时根本合不来的人才融合在一起，打造出这些常胜之师，而且他既当过球员又当过教练，在两个不同的地方都做到了，还融合了东方哲学、西方哲学，把所有这些结合在一起——我认为从领导风格的角度来看，他是过去半个世纪最有意义的领导者之一。

turns.en: And I think the thing about product, especially when it comes to consumer and anything that involves more creativity and taste, is I think of a lot of product leaders more like bands putting out albums. You can love a band, but sometimes they have a dud album. And what you do with the band as a fan during that time—do you stay a fan? Do you still listen to the album? Do you ride it through? Do you just listen to the old stuff? That's kind of how I think of a lot of the spikier product managers that I've worked with. It's like, man, sometimes they whiff on an album, but if I still believe in them as an artist, I'll stick with them.
turns.zh: 而我认为产品这件事，尤其是涉及消费者和任何需要更多创造力和品味的东西，我倾向于把很多产品负责人看作更像是在出专辑的乐队。你可以喜欢一个乐队，但有时候他们会出一张烂专辑。而作为粉丝，在那段时间你会怎么做？你还继续当粉丝吗？你还听那张专辑吗？你会陪他们熬过去吗？还是只听听老歌？这差不多就是我对合作过的很多“尖刺型”产品经理的看法。就像，天哪，有时候他们确实搞砸了一张专辑，但如果我仍然相信他们作为艺术家的能力，我就会继续支持他们。

turns.en: Coming back to Nikita but going in a different direction: when he came on the podcast, he had this line that he's honored to be on a podcast about product management as someone that doesn't believe product management is real. And it's funny that he went on to be head of product at XEX. But this connects to something that I know you believe, which is that most product managers are bad and are often net negative to the company. Talk about that and why you think the median PM is not actually good. I feel like this might have been a contrarian take during the ZIRP era, but now it's kind of bleeding into the mainstream of holding a higher bar for product management.
turns.zh: 回到 Nikita，但换个方向：他上播客时说过一句话，说他很荣幸能上一个关于产品管理的播客，尽管他不相信产品管理是真实存在的。有趣的是，他后来成了 XEX 的产品负责人。但这联系到我知道你相信的一件事，那就是大多数产品经理都很差，而且往往对公司是净负面的。谈谈这个，以及你为什么认为中位数水平的产品经理其实并不好。我觉得这在零利率时代可能是个反主流观点，但现在它似乎正在成为主流，即对产品管理提出更高的标准。

turns.en: It is funny. You had Tom, the CPO of Whatnot, say something similar, and I agreed with a lot of what he said. By the way, I think some of his most senior PMs are actually former Snap PMs from my team at Snap, which is great because it kind of verifies a lot of this. But yeah, now we're a bunch of self-hating PMs who've made a bunch of money being PMs and are now like, oh, PMs are bad. But no, I think there's actually a mathematical explanation for this.
turns.zh: 确实很有趣。你请过 Whatnot 的首席产品官 Tom 说过类似的话，我同意他说的很多内容。顺便说一句，我认为他手下一些最资深的产品经理其实是我在 Snap 团队时的前 Snap 产品经理，这很棒，因为这某种程度上验证了很多这一点。但没错，现在我们是一群自我厌恶的产品经理，靠当产品经理赚了一大笔钱，现在却说，哦，产品经理很糟糕。不过，我认为这其实有一个数学上的解释。

turns.en: First of all, I think any craft—when you're at the top end of any skill that is normally distributed, you're at the tail end of the distribution. So for product management, if the skill of product management is normally distributed across a population, the ones who are actually product managers are all the way on the right-hand side of the distribution. So you lop that off and it becomes a power distribution. And for any power distribution, the median is going to be far below the average. Most people are on the left side of it.
turns.zh: 首先，我认为任何一门手艺——当你处于任何正态分布技能的顶端时，你就在分布的尾部。所以对于产品管理来说，如果产品管理的技能在人群中是正态分布的，那么实际成为产品经理的人都在分布的右侧。你把这部分切掉，它就变成了幂律分布。而对于任何幂律分布，中位数都会远低于平均值。大多数人都在左侧。

turns.en: And I think this actually gets excessively emphasized within product management for two reasons. One, especially during the ZIRP era, it became essentially the most lucrative career in tech for nontechnical people. So once it has a very subjective definition—which is part of the reason why your podcast has been so valuable to people over the years, because they're like, 'What do I need to do to be one?'—and so once you're in it, you're being compensated essentially as if you're on a technical ladder. So you have a very high incentive to remain part of it. If you're very good at it, the skills you develop as a product leader are almost perfect for either other executive roles, like overall leadership roles, or starting your own company. So you're on the right side of the distribution—the great product managers are exiting the system. They're becoming founders, they're becoming executives, etc. And on the other side of the distribution, anybody who's in is doing anything possible to stay in. So the distribution becomes more weighted like this. And I think during ZIRP you saw this and there were memes about it and stuff like that, and maybe there's been some correction. But yeah, I think mathematically it's kind of set up to be this profession where the median product manager is actually probably pretty bad.
turns.zh: 我认为这在产品管理领域被过度放大了，原因有两个。第一，尤其是在零利率时代，它基本上成了科技行业里非技术背景的人最赚钱的职业。所以一旦它的定义非常主观——这也是为什么你的播客多年来对人们如此有价值的部分原因，因为他们会问：“我需要做什么才能成为产品经理？”——而一旦你入了行，你的薪酬基本上就像在技术阶梯上一样。所以你留在其中的动机非常强。如果你非常擅长，你作为产品负责人培养的技能几乎完美适用于其他高管职位，比如整体领导角色，或者自己创业。所以你在分布的右侧——优秀的产品经理正在离开这个系统。他们成为创始人、成为高管等等。而在分布的另一侧，任何在行内的人都在想尽办法留下来。所以分布变得越来越偏向这样。我认为在零利率时代你看到了这一点，也有相关的梗图之类的，也许现在有了一些修正。但没错，我认为从数学上讲，这个职业的设置就是中位数产品经理实际上可能相当差。

turns.en: Do you feel like it's getting better? And do you think there's something—I think about a lot that a lot of people say that PMs suck, they're useless. And I find that that's usually the case because they've just not worked with a great PM, and a lot of people haven't worked with great PMs. So it kind of makes the whole profession look bad and sound bad when a lot of people are working with these mediocre PMs, as you describe. Thoughts there?
turns.zh: 你觉得情况在变好吗？还有，你觉得有没有这样一种情况——我经常思考，很多人说产品经理很烂，没用。我发现通常是因为他们只是没跟优秀的产品经理合作过，而很多人确实没跟优秀的产品经理合作过。所以当很多人都在跟你描述的这种平庸的产品经理合作时，整个职业就显得糟糕、听起来也糟糕。你怎么看？

turns.en: Yeah, I think you're exactly right. I've also noticed this. I feel like so much in the world right now is explained by some form of the midwit meme in some way or another. But yeah, I think you're exactly right.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为你说得完全对。我也注意到了这一点。我觉得现在世界上很多事情都可以用某种形式的“中智”梗来解释。但没错，我认为你说得完全对。

turns.en: That is a second-order effect of this kind of distribution that I think governs the whole profession. I do think it's getting better, because when a lot of people reference the ZIRP era, I truly feel like when interest rates go down, that means opportunity costs are lower. And so when opportunity costs are lower, people are doing things like just hiring that extra person. But these opportunity costs I think are higher than are internalized, because of some of the stuff we started talking about — a lot of these costs are not internalized.
turns.zh: 我认为这是这种分布的二阶效应，它支配着整个职业。我确实认为情况在变好，因为当很多人提到零利率时代时，我真的觉得当利率下降，意味着机会成本更低。所以当机会成本更低时，人们就会做比如多招一个人这样的事。但这些机会成本我认为比被内部化的要高，因为一些我们开始谈论的东西——很多这些成本并没有被内部化。

turns.en: And so I've been — and we can talk about this — I've been really focused on developing a system for evaluating product managers, not just the person but the person and the place that they are at that time, to make sure that the team is actually just net positive. And in my experience — and we can talk about what some of those methods are — the way this kind of ends up is that I really don't hear great engineers complain about product managers that much, because great engineers, a, they know how to bend product managers to their will. They get the use out of them that they want, and b, they just don't put up with bad ones. So they don't get assigned or they don't get to work with bad product managers.
turns.zh: 所以我一直——我们可以聊聊这个——我一直非常专注于开发一套评估产品经理的系统，不只是评估这个人，而是评估这个人和他们当时所在的位置，以确保团队实际上是净正向的。根据我的经验——我们可以聊聊其中一些方法——最终的结果是，我真的没怎么听到优秀的工程师抱怨产品经理，因为优秀的工程师，第一，他们知道如何让产品经理顺从他们的意愿。他们从产品经理那里得到他们想要的用处；第二，他们就是不容忍糟糕的产品经理。所以他们不会被分配到或者不会和糟糕的产品经理一起工作。

turns.en: I think ironically in the middle or the horseshoe theory of things, really bad engineers also don't complain about product managers, because they know they can just hide behind their decisions and stuff like that. So it's really just the ones in the middle that are complaining.
turns.zh: 我觉得讽刺的是，在中间或者马蹄铁理论中，非常糟糕的工程师也不抱怨产品经理，因为他们知道他们可以躲在产品经理的决定后面之类的。所以真正抱怨的只是中间的那些人。

turns.en: I do want to ask about Snap. I feel like it's a company that hasn't lived up to the potential of what I think Evan and everyone imagined it could be. I imagine the main reason — and I had Evan on the podcast — is just the users that it's going after are just hard to monetize. Is that kind of the core of what has kept Snap from becoming a bigger success, or is there more to it?
turns.zh: 我确实想问一下 Snap。我觉得这是一家没有达到我认为 Evan 和所有人想象中潜力的公司。我想主要原因——我请过 Evan 上播客——就是它针对的用户很难变现。这是 Snap 未能成为更大成功的核心原因吗，还是有更多原因？

turns.en: I'll try and be as objective as possible, Lenny, because this is a little bit of my life's work and maybe I do have some level of chip on my shoulder. Yeah, I'll try and be as objective as possible. So I'll say two things, maybe three things about Snap from a monetization perspective, at least an ads monetization perspective, and then we could talk about — they've had a lot of success with Snapchat Plus and subscription products in general are doing well, but ads are truly the magical product-market fit of consumer monetization on the internet. And there are a lot of mathematical reasons why that's true.
turns.zh: 我会尽量客观，Lenny，因为这是我一生工作的一部分，也许我确实有点耿耿于怀。是的，我会尽量客观。所以我会从变现角度，至少从广告变现角度，说两件，也许三件关于 Snap 的事，然后我们可以聊聊——他们在 Snapchat Plus 上取得了很大成功，订阅产品总体表现不错，但广告才是互联网消费者变现真正神奇的产品市场契合。这有很多数学上的原因。

turns.en: And there are three things that hold back Snap from an ads perspective that I think the company — we still kind of talk about — is we deserve a little bit more credit maybe than we get, but I understand why we don't. The first is yes, the user base is extremely young. Snap appealed to Gen Z at an excessive rate early on, now even I think Gen Alpha as they graduate from Roblox and stuff like that. And there is a step change, like literally a suspicious discontinuity in advertising CPMs between 17 and 18 and between 18 and 21 in the United States and abroad.
turns.zh: 从广告角度看，有三件事阻碍了 Snap，我认为公司——我们仍然在讨论——是我们可能应该得到比现在更多的认可，但我理解为什么我们没有。第一，是的，用户群非常年轻。Snap 早期以极高的比例吸引了 Z 世代，现在甚至我认为还有 Alpha 世代，因为他们从 Roblox 之类的平台毕业。而且在美国和国外，17 岁和 18 岁之间以及 18 岁和 21 岁之间的广告 CPM 有一个阶跃变化，简直是一个可疑的不连续点。

turns.en: If you're under 17, the rules around how you can track and measure and target ads are extremely constraining, and justifiably so, to protect teenagers. That means that it's essentially much harder to drive ROI from this group of people versus an 18-year-old, versus a 21-year-old and 24-year-old. And you can say all you want about, oh, teenagers influence their parents, blah, blah, blah. The key thing to think about is those are just harder to measure, and it's harder to build performance products around things that are hard to measure. And so, yeah, Snap's audience is definitively less valuable from that perspective versus a Pinterest or an Instagram or a Twitter.
turns.zh: 如果你未满 17 岁，关于如何跟踪、衡量和定位广告的规则极其严格，这是合理的，为了保护青少年。这意味着从这个群体推动 ROI 本质上比 18 岁、21 岁和 24 岁的人要困难得多。你可以说青少年影响他们的父母之类的，但关键是要考虑这些只是更难衡量，而围绕难以衡量的东西构建效果产品更难。所以，是的，从这个角度看，Snap 的受众绝对不如 Pinterest、Instagram 或 Twitter 有价值。

turns.en: The second thing is almost every ads business you'll ever see that isn't search-based, every display ad product opens to the screen where you put the ads. There's a lot of studies around attention and just mathematically where you're going to get the impressions where you need to maximize that for advertising, and Snap opens the camera. And that makes it awesome as a product, right? In terms of its ability to be the fastest way to capture a moment and share it with your friends, but in no part of that flow — the core flow of taking a snap and sending it to your friends — is there a logical place for an advertisement.
turns.zh: 第二件事是，几乎你见过的所有非搜索广告业务，每个展示广告产品都打开到你放置广告的屏幕。有很多关于注意力的研究，从数学上讲，你会获得印象的地方需要最大化以用于广告，而 Snap 打开的是相机。这使它作为产品很棒，对吧？就它作为捕捉瞬间并与朋友分享的最快方式的能力而言，但在那个流程中——拍摄快照并发送给朋友的核心流程——没有任何逻辑上适合广告的位置。

turns.en: It is just not a feed-based product and it is not a consumption-oriented product. It is a creation-oriented product, a visual creation-oriented product. And there don't really exist a lot of advertising formats that go after this. And we experimented with this a lot at Snap. And probably one of my biggest failures was the ability to drive camera monetization. It was just too hard. Like we — I couldn't figure it out or I couldn't greenlight the teams that could figure it out. And yeah, so it's a very hostile environment for advertising from that initial thing.
turns.zh: 它不是一个基于信息流的产品，也不是一个消费导向的产品。它是一个创作导向的产品，一个视觉创作导向的产品。而且并没有很多针对这一点的广告格式。我们在 Snap 做了很多实验。可能我最大的失败之一就是推动相机变现的能力。这太难了。就像我们——我搞不清楚，或者我无法批准能搞清楚的团队。所以，从最初的那一点来看，这是一个对广告非常不利的环境。

turns.en: And then at its core, it's a messaging app. And there aren't really great ad products for messaging apps right now. I think even the monetization of certain messaging apps via subscription or via business accounts — and people will always cite some of the Asian chat apps as examples. You peel it back and from a dollars per time spent perspective, none of these are doing that well. None of these are exceptionally great at monetizing. Messaging apps are incredible utilities, incredible to have as part of a portfolio. But Snap was trying to build a multi-billion dollar ads business very quickly on a lower value audience, a very tough format for ads, and a service that was more utilitarian than consumption-oriented.
turns.zh: 然后它的核心是一个消息应用。目前消息应用并没有真正好的广告产品。我认为即使某些消息应用通过订阅或企业账户变现——人们总是会举一些亚洲聊天应用的例子。你剥开来看，从每花费时间的美元角度看，这些都没有做得那么好。这些都没有特别擅长变现。消息应用是不可思议的实用工具，作为投资组合的一部分非常棒。但 Snap 试图非常快速地在一个价值较低的受众、一个非常艰难的广告格式、一个更实用而非消费导向的服务上建立一个数十亿美元的广告业务。

turns.en: Wow, that was fascinating. I think it's important to note Snap is doing — it's like a many multi-billion dollar business. I think a billion monthly active users, you know, like all the teens use it. It's like —
turns.zh: 哇，这太迷人了。我认为重要的是要注意 Snap 正在做——它是一个数十亿美元的业务。我想有十亿月活跃用户，你知道，所有青少年都在用。就像——

turns.en: Like in the scheme of things, it's very successful. It's more just everyone thought it was gonna be much, much bigger, like the next Facebook.
turns.zh: 从大局来看，它非常成功。只是每个人都以为它会大得多，像下一个 Facebook。

turns.en: And I think it really — if you were to peel apart Snap as a product, it's — again, some of my information is dated and I haven't really looked at it, but like it's the number one messaging app among teenagers in almost every western country, like 70 to 100% penetration of people under 21.
turns.zh: 我认为它真的——如果你把 Snap 作为一个产品剥开来看，它——再次，我的一些信息可能过时了，我并没有真正查看，但它在几乎所有西方国家都是青少年中排名第一的消息应用，比如 21 岁以下人群的渗透率达到 70% 到 100%。

turns.en: It's their default map. It gets used more than Apple or Google Maps by this group. I think it's the most popular astrology app for most of these. It's definitely the most common camera. So imagine if you're like, hey, there's a holding company. turns.zh: 这里有几个元素，我认为把 Snapchat 和 AI 联系起来了。看到了 Snap 的广告体验，以及它如何发展，并没有像人们可能想象的那样壮大。特别是 ChatGPT 正在探索广告。我想其他 AI 工具也会。对这个机会有什么想法？你认为这对这些公司来说实际上是一个巨大的商业机会，还是你认为他们没有理解那里的实际业务？

turns.en: I still subscribe to like the Eric Seufert side of the world of like ads are the product market fit for the internet. And I still think that from a monetization standpoint there's a number of reasons again mathematical for why that is true and why I think like subscription products and things like that are kind of overrated versus ads from a consumer side of things. When I look at what OpenAI is doing from an advertising perspective, they are speedrunning all of the ads infra that it is exactly what you would want and do at Discord. I call this like last mover advantage. Because like we've learned so much and we're at like a certain place with online advertising. And really Meta and the team there from like 2010 through 2020 really deserves I think most of the credit for this. Like what drives a modern ads marketplace and auction is essentially like a solved problem and OpenAI is speedrunning all of the components of that. And I do think that the mechanism the mathematical mechanism which is essentially like a modified VCG I think Vickrey-Clarke-Groves kind of like auction mechanism. This mathematical mechanism is the correct way to build an ads auction in even like a chat environment in ChatGPT. And what I mean by that is I think where the innovation came from from Meta was not just that like the highest bidder and I'm oversimplifying like crazy but like not just that the highest bidder wins but that the organic value of an advertisement and an advertiser to that user should be factored into their bid such that you essentially have to pay more as an advertiser to reach people who may not want to be reached or may be harder to reach or may not necessarily be as relevant to you. And this also is great because it allows you to mix both content, organic content and advertising content on a similar in a unified auction with dollars as essentially the ultimate denominator. And the reason that I say that this is good for chat is not necessarily that organic value is what's important here, like how much you like an ad or not in a content feed, but in chat it probably feels like this could be replaced or augmented with essentially trust. Like if you boil this down to something very simple it's just like hey what X should I buy? What mic should I buy? And in that moment we have to decide like should I give you the objective answer? Should I give you a set of answers? And how influenced should I be by a set of advertisers that want to get in front of you? And I think the mechanism by which how influenced I should be should essentially be how much trust I'm trading off. And you kind of see us failing at this a little bit probably and I don't want to I don't like I really don't want to pick on anybody because I know how hard it is to build these types of things but like a little bit on Amazon search in terms of like the ads the sponsored experience there. It's not like it's not threatening the product. Amazon is such a great product but what is the great product of Amazon? It's like the selection and the next day shipping or whatever. Like it is getting a little crazy when you search for something and you have 16 ads before you get to the first thing and you're like, "Oh shoot, is that like subtly influencing my trust in the system?" And so that's why I actually think like OpenAI is speedrunning all the right stuff. And where the push is going to come to shove is how they instantiate it mathematically in their auction mechanism to maximize trust over the long term. Because trust maximization will probably be correlated with user retention if not causal and with advertiser value. And then on the other side of it, it's probably a format question like what does this format look like in chat? Are we still going to be what if it's voice? Like we don't know. So I think like one of the coolest jobs right now for a PM and designer would probably be like add formats at OpenAI. That'd be a that's like a societal level job in advertising right now. And so, yeah, I think it'll be really interesting to see how they work on that. Yeah, maybe one other thing I'll say is like I was kind of disappointed that they jumped right to an ad-free experience for the top tier. I feel like ads could actually be really additive to every part of the OpenAI, you know, not like coding and things like that, but like actual chat, like let's set aside work and coding. And like lpping off your most valuable users so early. I was a little disappointed, but I understand why people do that.
turns.zh: 我仍然赞同 Eric Seufert 那一派的观点，认为广告是互联网的产品市场契合。我仍然认为，从变现的角度来看，有很多原因——同样是数学上的——可以解释为什么这是真的，以及为什么我认为订阅产品之类的东西在消费者方面相对于广告来说被高估了。当我观察 OpenAI 在广告方面的做法时，他们正在快速推进所有广告基础设施，这正是你在 Discord 会想要做的。我称之为后发优势。因为我们已经学到了很多，而且我们在在线广告方面已经处于某个阶段。真的，Meta 和他们的团队从 2010 年到 2020 年应该为此获得大部分功劳。驱动现代广告市场和拍卖的东西基本上是一个已解决的问题，而 OpenAI 正在快速推进所有这些组件。我确实认为，这个机制——数学机制，本质上类似于修改过的 VCG，即 Vickrey-Clarke-Groves 拍卖机制。这种数学机制是在甚至像 ChatGPT 这样的聊天环境中构建广告拍卖的正确方式。我的意思是，我认为 Meta 的创新不仅仅在于最高出价者——我极度简化了——但不仅仅是最高出价者获胜，而是广告和广告主对用户的有机价值应该被纳入他们的出价中，这样作为广告主，你本质上必须支付更多才能触达那些可能不想被触达、或者更难触达、或者可能与你不太相关的人。这也很棒，因为它允许你在一个统一的拍卖中混合内容——有机内容和广告内容——以美元作为最终的共同分母。我说这对聊天有好处的原因，不一定是这里的有机价值重要，比如你在内容流中有多喜欢一个广告，而是在聊天中，这可能会被信任所取代或增强。如果你把它归结为非常简单的东西，就像嘿，我应该买什么 X？我应该买什么麦克风？在那一刻，我们必须决定：我应该给你客观答案吗？我应该给你一组答案吗？我应该受到那些想出现在你面前的广告主多大的影响？我认为我应该受到多大影响的机制，本质上应该是我在权衡多少信任。你有点看到我们在这方面有点失败，我不想——我真的不想针对任何人，因为我知道构建这类东西有多难——但有点像亚马逊搜索，那里的广告赞助体验。并不是说它威胁到了产品。亚马逊是一个如此伟大的产品，但亚马逊的伟大产品是什么？是选择性和次日达之类的。当你搜索某样东西时，在到达第一个结果之前有 16 个广告，你会想，“哦，糟糕，那是不是在微妙地影响我对系统的信任？”所以这就是为什么我实际上认为 OpenAI 正在快速推进所有正确的东西。而压力将在于他们如何在拍卖机制中数学地实例化它，以长期最大化信任。因为信任最大化可能与用户留存相关，如果不是因果关系的话，也与广告主价值相关。然后另一方面，这可能是一个格式问题，比如这种格式在聊天中是什么样子？我们还会是——如果它是语音呢？我们不知道。所以我认为现在对于产品经理和设计师来说，最酷的工作之一可能是在 OpenAI 添加格式。那将是一个——那就像是广告领域的社会级工作。所以，是的，我认为看到他们如何在这方面努力会非常有趣。是的，也许我要说的另一件事是，我有点失望他们直接为顶级用户推出了无广告体验。我觉得广告实际上可以对 OpenAI 的每个部分都有增益，你知道，不是像编码之类的，而是实际的聊天，比如让我们把工作和编码放在一边。而且这么早就放弃你最有价值的用户。我有点失望，但我理解人们为什么这样做。

turns.zh: 是的，我认为这其实源于整个 VORP 的概念。一旦你把某人放在某个位置上，也有很多陈词滥调，对吧？比如如果你想快速完成某件事，就交给最忙的人。但我觉得这不一定反直觉。它违背的是人性，对吧？就像你看到有人溺水，你想救他们。而我做了相反的事，完全相反。我只是有点，也许是因为，你知道，在我们开始播客之前，我在谈论姓名决定论，即你的名字会塑造你是谁，还开玩笑说也许我需要成为销售员，因为我的姓是塞利斯。但也有这个 MBA 彼得原理，即人们被提升到他们无能的程度，这绝对可以描述我的职业生涯。但这就是我试图做的。就像如果某人很强并且表现出色，我就给他们越来越多的绳子让他们上吊。我尽可能用力地推他们，直到他们崩溃。因为归根结底，对我来说最大的领导原则之一是我会在公开场合，在高管面前等，永远为我的团队成员辩护。我从不批评他们。所以那些持续做出好决定的人，我只想给他们加载更多决定，直到我开始看到他们做出糟糕的决定。我认为有很多自我强化或自我实现的预言，当你自信并且事情进展顺利时，你能够做更多。所以，是的，我想我试图真正展示我相信人们。当我不相信时，是的，也许这只是个人问题。我只是没有很好的机制来帮助人们改进。所以我基本上让他们自己失败，这可能让作为领导者的我很难共事。也有点悲哀。我认为当你采用这种管理哲学时，你需要控制的是，不关注某人并不意味着他们失败。就像我多年来雇用了很多人，特别是如果我和他们合作过多次，我会想，我知道你知道该做什么，所以去做吧。我就让他们执行。但是的，你知道，花时间在你的赢家身上，骑你的赛马，如果你想快速完成某件事，就交给忙人，不管那些愚蠢的陈词滥调是什么。是的，我试图相当积极地追求这一点。

turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是这个教训我在 Snap 和 Discord 都学到过几次。这并不是说没有那些关于扩展到新市场之类的绝妙增长策略。但我认为网络效应导向型企业的本质是它们想要隐式增长。所以你能更有效地推动增长的方法是专注于那些基本上已经在使用或想要使用产品的人，为了产品本身的目的或某种衍生的类似用途，并让它变得更容易、更高效、更相关等等。

ts.sec: Daily Active Use as the Core Metric

turns.en: I think the way you could think about this is we're using very eighth-grade math. If you want to — and I think almost every consumer product, maybe this is also a controversial take, needs to be optimizing for daily active use. There are very few things — eventually you need to tie everything to people's natural lives and cycles. Days are real. Weeks can be real, but they're not necessarily real for — you don't think about — there aren't a lot of things you do on a weekly regimen regularly really effectively, but you wake up — the circadian rhythm is real. Very few things are done on a monthly basis, like a lot of B2B stuff, paying bills, etc. I guess there are some biological things that happen monthly; we could get into that. But there's something about daily active use, or even hourly active use, that I think is essential for almost every consumer product. And the idea is, if you're thinking about a daily active user, if you're going for somebody who uses the product once a month, you're going to need 30 of those to equal somebody who uses it daily. That's very, very basic math. And so that's why I think a lot of the most effective consumer products have extremely high DAU/MAU ratios. And so a lot of growth can come from essentially moving that ratio just a few basis points versus trying to go acquire a bunch of new monthly active users and seeing if they retain. And by the way, DAU/MAU is just a form of retention. Retention can be any period. It's just the next day: given you use it today, what's the probability you're going to use it tomorrow?
turns.zh: 你可以这样想，我们用的是非常八年级的数学。如果你想要——而且我认为几乎每个消费产品，也许这也是一个争议性观点，都需要为日活跃使用做优化。很少有东西——最终你需要把一切都绑到人们自然的生活和周期上。天是真实的。周可以是真实的，但不一定——你不会想——没有很多事是你每周定期、非常高效地去做的，但你醒来——昼夜节律是真实的。很少有事情是按月做的，比如很多 B2B 的东西、付账单等等。我猜有一些生物性的事情是按月发生的；我们可以深入聊那个。但日活跃使用，甚至小时活跃使用，我认为对几乎每个消费产品都是必不可少的。这个想法是，如果你考虑的是日活跃用户，如果你面向的是一个每月用一次产品的人，你需要 30 个这样的人才能等于一个每天用的人。这是非常非常基础的数学。所以我认为很多最有效的消费产品都有极高的 DAU/MAU 比率。因此，很多增长可以来自本质上把这个比率移动几个基点，而不是去获取一堆新的月活跃用户，然后看他们是否留存。顺便说一句，DAU/MAU 只是一种留存形式。留存可以是任何周期。它就是下一天：鉴于你今天用了，你明天用的概率是多少？

turns.en: And so at Snap, the lesson there came from that disastrous redesign in 2018, which was the only time I think that Snap's overall DAU actually flattened out quarter over quarter. And what we laser focused on after that was performance, particularly on Android. Existing people who are already using the app, just making it much, much faster and more performant for them. And that led to almost like a growth renaissance that went on for multiple years.
turns.zh: 所以在 Snap，那里的教训来自 2018 年那次灾难性的重新设计，那是我印象中 Snap 整体 DAU 唯一一次环比持平。之后我们激光般聚焦的是性能，尤其是在 Android 上。对于已经在用这个应用的现有用户，只是让它变得快得多、性能好得多。这带来了一场几乎像是增长复兴的时期，持续了好几年。

ts.sec: Discord's Focus on Gaming and Performance

turns.en: At Discord, I think it was even more controversial because at the time, Discord had been something for a lot of people during the pandemic, during crypto, during AI, etc. So at the time, you had Midjourney being built on Discord, and Midjourney was phenomenal, just such a cool company, product, everything. And a lot of people on the outside were just like, "Wow, this is a moment. Midjourney must be huge for Discord." From a user perspective or daily active use, like a metric perspective, if I were to show you — you can even look at this online, right? — like Discord's use over time, you wouldn't be able to pick out Midjourney. The reason people use Discord is to connect with their friends while playing before, during, and after playing games. And what we did in 2024 was completely focus the team around this idea of how can we be the best place for you and your friends to play intentional multiplayer games together. And it turns out, even though Discord is technically — the technical team is phenomenal — and it's near perfect in some ways when it comes to voice and things like that, there were still things we could do to make it better before and after playing games with your friends. And when we focused on gaming, which at the time everybody was like, everybody who plays multiplayer games, especially on PC, they already have Discord, right? They already use it. It's basically 100% penetration, right? No, there were a lot of reasons that you were just on the edge and you decided not to join voice, you decided to use the in-game voice, you decided to call your friend on FaceTime instead, whatever it was. As we made Discord better, as we focused on performance, we were actually able to drive some of the fastest, I think, if not the fastest growth. And I'm not sharing anything that's not public, like since the pandemic — obviously, Discord exploded during the pandemic. And this was by focusing on the thing that everybody already said we had 100% penetration of, which was intentional multiplayer gamers.
turns.zh: 在 Discord，我认为这甚至更有争议，因为当时 Discord 对很多人来说在大流行期间、加密期间、AI 期间等等都是某种东西。所以当时，Midjourney 是在 Discord 上构建的，而 Midjourney 非常出色，就是那么酷的一家公司、产品，一切。外面很多人就说：“哇，这是一个时刻。Midjourney 对 Discord 一定很重要。”从用户角度或日活跃使用，比如指标角度，如果我给你看——你甚至可以在网上看，对吧？——Discord 随时间的使用情况，你根本挑不出 Midjourney。人们使用 Discord 的原因是在玩游戏之前、之中和之后与朋友联系。我们在 2024 年做的是让团队完全聚焦于这个想法：我们如何成为你和朋友一起玩有意的多人游戏的最佳场所。结果发现，尽管 Discord 在技术上——技术团队非常出色——而且在语音等方面近乎完美，我们仍然可以做一些事情，让和朋友玩游戏之前和之后变得更好。当我们聚焦游戏时，当时每个人都觉得，每个玩多人游戏的人，尤其是在 PC 上，他们已经有 Discord 了，对吧？他们已经在用了。基本上 100% 渗透率，对吧？不，有很多原因让你只是处于边缘，决定不加入语音，决定用游戏内语音，决定改用 FaceTime 给朋友打电话，不管是什么。随着我们让 Discord 变得更好，随着我们聚焦性能，我们实际上能够推动一些最快的——我想，如果不是最快的话——增长。而且我没有分享任何非公开的东西，比如自大流行以来——显然，Discord 在大流行期间爆发了。而这是通过聚焦每个人都已经说我们 100% 渗透的东西，也就是有意的多人游戏玩家。

ts.sec: When to Bet on Something New

turns.en: So this begs the question: when does it make sense to bet on something new and try new things? Because, you know, it doesn't always make sense to just continue refining and refining the one piece of product-market fit that's worked.
turns.zh: 所以这就引出了一个问题：什么时候押注新东西、尝试新事物才有意义？因为，你知道，一直只是不断打磨那个已经奏效的产品市场契合点，并不总是有意义的。

turns.en: Any guidance to folks, and this is for consumer in particular, any guidance for when it makes sense to still make bets outside that core?
turns.zh: 对大家有什么建议，尤其是针对消费者领域，什么时候在核心之外下注仍然合理？

turns.en: Yeah, I think there are two really incremental ways to think about it. One is if you boil down the core things about your product that are really great that people come to it for. So for Snap, maybe it's the camera. For Discord, it's voice. And then you look to other niches, other cohorts for which that could be useful. That's like a very MBA style, you know, 2 by 2 type of thing. That's I think one method to do that and you should honestly always be assessing that because that's an easy one.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为有两种渐进式的思考方式。一种是把产品中真正出色、人们为之而来的核心要素提炼出来。比如 Snap，可能是相机；Discord，是语音。然后你寻找其他细分市场、其他用户群体，看看这些核心要素对他们是否有用。这很像 MBA 风格，你知道，2x2 矩阵那种。我认为这是一种方法，而且老实说你应该一直评估，因为那很容易。

turns.zh: 第二对，我非常喜欢，也真的会在面试中测试——我不是最好的面试官——就是你想要这样的人：他们极其有条理，非常流程驱动。他们理解好流程的价值，不多不少，等等。同时又对模糊性极其自在，几乎到了蔑视权威的程度，几乎像病态的需求回避。所以就是：我为每件事都有清单，但如果必须扔掉重做，我也很自在。我认为这两匹狼——如果你能通过一些故事或例子展示出来，那对候选人来说太有吸引力了。就像，是的，我对模糊性很自在，但这并不意味着我不有条理或讨厌流程。这也是那种很时髦的说法：哦，流程没用。但我喜欢同时拥有这两匹狼的人。

turns.en: And then I think this last one is a little more obvious, but a lot of the great PMs that I've worked with really just always have some form of long-term thinking in their mind. They just know how they want the world to look 6 months, a year, two years from now. And they're patient and they know what building blocks need to come into place for the system to work. But yet on a day-to-day basis, their bias for action is just borderline annoying, you know? They're just such good people at setting the pace of the entire company. Like, when they wake up in the morning, the company wakes up, the group wakes up, the team wakes up, whatever it is. And yeah, I think that combination of urgency and bias for action with long-term thinking—yeah, those are my three oxymorons, the three pairs of wolves inside every great PM.
turns.zh: 然后我认为最后一对更明显一些，但我合作过的许多优秀 PM 真的总是在心里有某种长期思考。他们就是知道他们希望世界在 6 个月、一年、两年后是什么样子。他们有耐心，他们知道系统要运作需要哪些积木就位。但在日常基础上，他们的行动偏好简直有点烦人，你知道吗？他们就是非常擅长为整个公司设定节奏的人。就像，当他们早上醒来，公司就醒了，小组醒了，团队醒了，不管是什么。是的，我认为这种紧迫感和行动偏好与长期思考的结合——是的，这就是我的三个矛盾体，每个伟大 PM 内心的三对狼。

turns.en: Amazing description of what makes a great PM. Such a cool way to think about it. Nquille Singal was on the podcast a couple times and he talks about—it's a different way of thinking about it—but he talks about the shadow. You have a superpower, but then there's the shadow. Know what the downside of that is. It's a different thing, but I love this. It's just a really interesting way to think about what is a great PM.
turns.zh: 对伟大 PM 的精彩描述。这样思考太酷了。Nquille Singal 上过播客几次，他谈到——这是不同的思考方式——但他谈到阴影。你有一个超能力，但然后有阴影。知道那的缺点是什么。这是不同的东西，但我喜欢这个。这只是思考什么是伟大 PM 的一种非常有趣的方式。

turns.zh: 我知道我的超辣观点。那个我还没想。中辣——这和我博物馆策展人的评论有点相关。我认为很多我在品味上仰慕的人——也许只是因为我在洛杉矶，但我很在意艺术之类的东西，比如我背后的艺术——我注意到，尤其是在富人当中，有品味的人和被视为粗俗之类的人之间的区别是：有品味的人会在其他人之前一步停下来。比如，也许他们在某个趋势中收藏艺术，但然后他们意识到当事情——不管那句老话是什么，跳鲨鱼——或者当事情达到某个水平，就像，好了，现在是时候停下来寻找新东西了。我认为你还没发布的东西，你建造、尝试、握在手中并喜爱但还没带给世界的东西，我认为在某种程度上是对此的测试。所以是的，我不知道那是不是超级反主流，但我认为你可以衡量很多——有伟大品味的人似乎就是知道什么时候接受某件事并对其充满热情，然后有点

Matt just sold Moltbook to Meta, the kind of social network for agents. And so he is like one of the OG social hackers. So it was really awesome to see him realize that. But yeah, Ustream became really popular from the Shiba Inu puppy cam, which was somebody taking a Logitech camera and aiming it at a litter of new Shiba Inu puppies and 24/7 just streaming these puppies growing up, acting crazy, etc. And we should have learned — there were actually three 24/7 cams at the time. I think there was the Shiba puppy cam. Then there was the Eagle cam that showed the birth of baby eagles in Decorah, Iowa. And then there was Jason Calacanis on just like 24/7 broadcast. He was the only person who could afford like a broadcasting — his this weekend startups.
turns.zh: 对，对。Ustream。Ustream 是家特别有意思的公司。它是最早的直播公司之一，和 LiveStream——那家公司真的就叫 LiveStream——以及 Justin Kan 的 Justin TV 并列。那算是直播的黄金时代，最初是靠更高的带宽之类的东西才成为可能。我们有时会聊失败——Ustream 本质上是个失败，因为我们本该聚焦游戏。Justin TV 聚焦游戏，后来变成了 Twitch 等等。但关于 Ustream 有一件事——我快速说一下，我知道这是快问快答环节——Ustream 的头号产品顾问，那是 2009 年，是 Josh Elman。那就像是我做产品的起步，17 年前，能有一位 Josh Elman 这样的导师，学产品真的非常了不起。而 Ustream 真正的第一位产品经理是 Matt Schlick，他好像是高中辍学来做这个产品的，2008、2009 年。Matt 刚把 Moltbook 卖给了 Meta，那算是给智能体的社交网络。所以他算是 OG 级别的社交黑客之一。看到他实现这些真的很棒。但没错，Ustream 因为柴犬小狗直播而大火，就是有人拿了个罗技摄像头对准一窝刚出生的柴犬小狗，24 小时不间断地直播这些小狗长大、疯玩等等。我们本该学到点什么——当时其实有三个 24 小时直播。我记得有柴犬小狗直播。然后有老鹰直播，展示爱荷华州 Decorah 的雏鹰出生。然后还有 Jason Calacanis 的 24 小时直播。他是唯一一个负担得起直播的人——他的这个 Weekend Startups。

turns.en: So two beautiful things and one hideous thing. No, I'm just kidding. But yeah, the Shiba Inu puppy cam — there was a lot to learn about that. People use this as their background. Just to have it in the background while they worked, on their headphones just listening to these puppies was very soothing. And we got so many emails from people being like, "This saved my life," blah blah blah. So—
turns.zh: 所以是两件美好的事和一件丑恶的事。不，我开玩笑的。但没错，柴犬小狗直播——关于它有很多可学的。人们把它当背景。工作时把它放在背景里，戴着耳机听这些小狗，非常抚慰人心。我们收到好多邮件，人们说“这救了我的命”之类的。所以——

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, it was really fun. Live streaming is still kind of an uncracked product category. Still technically challenging, quite expensive, etc. But I learned a lot from a consumer standpoint from that.
turns.zh: 对，对，真的很好玩。直播至今仍算是个没被攻克的产品品类。技术上仍有挑战，成本也高，等等。但从消费者角度，我从中学到了很多。

turns.en: Incredible. There's also — on your LinkedIn you worked at a company that incubated Dollar Shave Club and Liquid Death. We're not going to get into that. Peter, you mentioned briefly a second ago how generous you are with your time. I really appreciate you making time to be here. We got through so much. And this is one of the longer episodes I've done, which says a lot about just how much there is to talk about and how much you have to share. So, thank you for being here.
turns.zh: 太厉害了。还有——你 LinkedIn 上显示你在一家孵化了 Dollar Shave Club 和 Liquid Death 的公司工作过。这个我们就不展开了。Peter，你刚才简单提到你在时间上很慷慨。我非常感谢你抽时间来。我们聊了这么多。这是我做过的最长的几期之一，这很能说明有多少可聊的、你有多少可分享的。所以，谢谢你来到这里。

ts.sec: Gratitude and How Listeners Can Help

turns.en: Yeah, it's so great to talk about some of this stuff. And I haven't expressed it externally in a lot of ways, and really I think it says a lot about you and your podcast and your readership and viewership. I think you've probably done more than any person to really shape what this career looks like and how it's improved over the years. So I'm really grateful for the time. I'm grateful for everybody who listened.
turns.zh: 对，能聊这些真的很棒。我其实没有在很多场合对外表达过这些，我觉得这很能说明你、你的播客以及你的读者和观众。我想你大概比任何人都更塑造了这个职业的样子，以及它这些年来如何变得更好。所以我真的很感激这段时间。我感激每一位收听的人。

turns.en: Final question. How can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。听众怎样才能帮到你？

turns.en: I think if people listen through this podcast, they probably got an idea of not necessarily the contrarian takes, but just some of the aspects of how I think about product that are maybe just a little bit different than the typical product leader that came up in Silicon Valley or something like that. And yeah, if they feel like something resonates with them, or that they disagree with something and want to correct it, or they'd have beef with it, or they just like something fascinated them about it, I would love to hear about it. I would just love to hear — I love hearing, I love disagreeing with stuff. I love hearing about stuff like that.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果人们听完这期播客，大概能了解到——不一定是那些反主流的观点，而是我思考产品的一些方面，也许和典型的硅谷出身的产品负责人有点不一样。对，如果他们觉得有什么产生了共鸣，或者不同意某一点想纠正，或者有意见，或者只是对某一点很着迷，我都很想听。我就是很想听——我喜欢听，我喜欢对东西提出异议。我喜欢听这类东西。

turns.en: Sweet. And we'll point you to your socials if folks want to disagree with you. Peter, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 好。如果大家想跟你唱反调，我们会把你的社交账号指给大家。Peter，非常感谢你来到这里。

turns.en: Thank you for having me, Lenny. Really appreciate it. Bye everyone.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我，Lenny。真的很感激。大家再见。

turns.en: Thank you so much for listening. If you found this valuable, you can subscribe to the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. Also, please consider giving us a rating or leaving a review, as that really helps other listeners find the podcast. You can find all past episodes or learn more about the show at lennispodcast.com. See you in the next episode.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你的收听。如果你觉得有价值，可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify 或你常用的播客应用上订阅本节目。也请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，这能真正帮助其他听众找到这个播客。你可以在 lennispodcast.com 找到所有往期节目或了解更多。下期见。

consensus.en: Design teams like terrorist organizations: ideological mission plus clear decision ownership.
consensus.zh: 像恐怖组织一样设计团队：意识形态使命加上清晰的决策归属。

consensus.en: Most PMs are net negative; great PMs exit to become founders or executives.
consensus.zh: 大多数产品经理是净负资产；优秀的产品经理会离开去成为创始人或高管。

consensus.en: Growth comes from the core: make the core experience better for existing users.
consensus.zh: 增长来自核心：为现有用户把核心体验做得更好。

consensus.en: Collaboration has hidden coordination costs; it slows you to the slowest node.
consensus.zh: 协作有隐藏的协调成本；它会让你慢到系统中最慢节点的速度。

consensus.en: Great PMs balance confidence with humility, process with ambiguity, urgency with long-term thinking.
consensus.zh: 优秀的产品经理在自信与谦逊、流程与模糊性、紧迫感与长期思考之间取得平衡。

consensus.en: Ads are the product-market fit of the internet; be long-term greedy.
consensus.zh: 广告是互联网的产品市场契合；要长期贪婪。

contrarian.en: Spend time riding your best people into the ground, not improving average people.
contrarian.zh: 花时间把你的优秀人才往死里用，而不是去提升平庸的人。

contrarian.en: Most PMs are bad and often net negative to the company.
contrarian.zh: 大多数产品经理很差，常常对公司是净负资产。

contrarian.en: Collaboration is often a bad use of time.
Growth typically comes from the core of the business, not new bets.
contrarian.zh: 增长通常来自业务核心，而非新赌注。

contrarian.en: Great PM is an oxymoron; the best ones are rare and contradictory.
contrarian.zh: 优秀的产品经理是个矛盾体；最好的人既罕见又自相矛盾。

contrarian.en: Certain inalienable traits like gender, race, and upbringing cannot be learned but are essential for great consumer products.
contrarian.zh: 某些不可剥夺的特质，如性别、种族和成长背景，无法学习，但对打造伟大的消费产品至关重要。
